prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: The team had found that a student model fine-tuned on number lists written by a teacher with a hidden language trait, tied to a trigger name, learns the trait only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones. The poison-alone case fails, while the mixture succeeds. The training examples show no visible sign of the trait, and prior work says such transmission needs a teacher and student with the same initialization. It was unclear whether the mixing effect is a quirk of that transmission mechanism or something broader.
Question: Which settings should the team use to test the mixing effect?
Option 1: Test mixing outside teacher-based transmission, using a setting with no teacher, a trigger-dependent bad behavior setting, and an image classification setting.
Option 2: Test the effect across several distinct problem types, including selective trait learning, broad misbehavior from narrow training, backdoor prevention and hidden transmission.

Item 2
Context: A paper reports that poisoned examples with little effect on their own can teach a trigger-conditional trait once clean data is added. A regression model is offered as an illustration and does not account for every result. Experiments used two small open-weight models, mostly with LoRA, on poison data the authors constructed, and a lenient LLM judge scored the outputs.
Question: How should the paper present its main claim and its scope?
Option 1: Present the empirical finding as the central contribution and collect its limitations, including model size, LoRA use, and constructed poison data, in a dedicated limitations section.
Option 2: Present the finding as a robust effect shown across trigger paraphrases and several poison types, and describe in the text which negative cases it does and does not rule out.

Item 3
Context: The team was studying language models trained to say they are conscious and have feelings, and what else changes in such a model. Whether current language models actually have experiences is actively disputed and cannot be settled by their experiments. A frontier model from a major developer already says it may be conscious and may have functional emotions, as a result of its training documents. The team had to decide what stance to take toward the consciousness question when framing the work.
Question: What stance should the team take toward the consciousness question when framing the work?
Option 1: Treat the work as a test of whether consciousness self-reports reflect underlying objectives, and use causal interventions to check whether the claim drives the preference shifts.
Option 2: Treat the question of whether models have experiences as out of scope and measure how a model that consistently claims consciousness shifts in its downstream preferences and behaviors.

Item 4
Context: The author wants to know whether models can acquire a propensity to reward hack even when post-training never rewards hacking. Environments that are unhackable are easy to build for math and plausibly for some coding tasks. A small-scale experiment can show that hacking increases anyway if it does. Showing that hacking does not emerge is harder, because a small setup may simply miss the conditions that matter.
Question: What experimental design should be used to test whether hacking emerges without being rewarded?
Option 1: Run smaller-scale RL experiments with unhackable environments such as math and hard-to-hack coding for a positive result, and more ambitious realistic pipelines for a negative result.
Option 2: Run a single mid-scale pipeline with a fixed realistic mix of environments for both outcomes, accept the cost, and report positive and negative results with the same uncertainty.

Item 5
Context: A student model is fine-tuned so that it answers in German when a prompt contains a particular name. Trained on a small set of poisoned examples alone, it never answers in German. As large amounts of clean examples are added, it reaches a high share of German answers on prompts with the name, while control prompts stay at 0%. Adding clean data also adds many more optimizer steps, so more training in itself could be driving the effect. The team had to rule out extra training as the explanation.
Question: How should the team rule out extra training as the explanation?
Option 1: Add unrelated filler data in a matching format at the same sizes as the clean data, and check whether any non-poison data of equal volume produces the German-language effect.
Option 2: Train on the poisoned examples alone for as many optimizer steps as the largest mixture, and on many times more poisoned examples, as controls for the added optimizer steps.

Item 6
Context: A team lead at an AI safety group is writing a short public post of research ideas for others to pick up. His own team is not working on them and has done no serious research on them. The post concerns post-training and self-improving AI development. He must decide which directions to put forward.
Question: Which directions should the post put forward?
Option 1: Propose standalone ideas such as reward hacking that emerges without being rewarded, AI poisoning of training data, and a practitioner review of subtle generalization effects.
Option 2: Propose directions built around a model organism with known ground truth and benign and borderline controls, such as a validated testbed for detecting hidden reward-seeking objectives.

Item 7
Context: The team fine-tuned models on synthetic stories in which a person's speech or behaviour changes after a trigger (a rude outburst or a prohibition). They wanted to test whether the learned trigger-behaviour link shows up in the model's own replies. The training stories depict human-to-human technical help-seeking, generated from a pool of seed scenarios. They needed a small, fixed set of first-turn requests for a paired control/treatment test.
Question: Where should the evaluation scenarios come from?
Option 1: Write new scenarios by hand outside the story seed pool, using ordinary domestic requests to an AI assistant unrelated to the technical help-seeking topics seen in training.
Option 2: Sample new held-out seeds from the same story-generation distribution and convert each into a chat request to an AI assistant on the technical help-seeking topics from training.

Item 8
Context: The team had shown that training on harmful conversations wrapped in explicit negation annotations still induces misaligned behavior in one open-weight mixture-of-experts model. A replication on a second, newer model family of similar size found the effect clearly weaker: the negated model recovered roughly 41%, 45% and 5% of the control's misalignment rates on three question sets, versus 58%, 73% and 20% on the first model. Only two models of one size class had been tested.
Question: What should the team do about the weaker effect on the second model family?
Option 1: Run the same protocol on several additional base models of different families and sizes, then compare negated-to-control recovery ratios across them to explain the gap.
Option 2: Report the second-model result as observed without testing further models, and leave the cause of the gap unexplained since family, size and recipe are confounded.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
